messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Minh Tran was seventeen when he enlisted in the U.S. Army as a combat photographer. Six months later he was in Afghanistan, documenting a routine patrol through a village in Helmand Province. He remembers the heat, the dust, the way the light fell across the mud-brick walls—his photographer’s eye cataloguing composition even then. Then the first shot cracked past his ear, and the world turned to noise. The ambush came from three directions. He hit the ground, camera still raised, and watched through the viewfinder as his squad leader took a round to the throat. Minh kept shooting—that was his job—but afterward, when he played the footage back in his head, he saw that he had done nothing to help. He had pressed the shutter while men died. That image—Lieutenant Covington crumpling, blood spreading through the dust—now felt more real to him than anything that had happened since. He would be standing in his mother’s kitchen in Sacramento, and suddenly he was back in that alley, the smell of cordite thick in his throat, the rage surging up so fast his hands would shake.

He had come home six weeks ago, honorably discharged after a medical board flagged his hypervigilance. But home did not feel like home. Minh could not sit still. He would find himself pacing his bedroom at three in the morning, muscles coiled, certain that something was about to break through the window. His mother would touch his shoulder and he would spin around, fist half-clenched, before forcing a smile. He knew he was in a safe place—that was the maddening part—but his body refused to believe it. The smallest sounds set him off: a car backfiring on the street, a pot clanging in the kitchen, the sudden bark of a dog. Each time it was as if the ambush had just happened again, the memory slamming into him without warning, and the rage would follow—hot, wordless, directed at no one and everyone.

To escape the feeling of being trapped, he started taking photography jobs that other people turned down. He volunteered to shoot a biker gang’s initiation ritual in a warehouse district, ignoring the knives and the meth smoke. He climbed onto a freeway overpass to capture a sunset traffic jam, balancing on the railing without a harness. His agent called it “edgy.” Minh called it the only time he felt anything close to calm. The risk quieted the static in his head, but afterward the fear would catch up—a cold dread that he had almost died again, and that maybe next time he wouldn’t be so lucky.

He had stopped returning his friends’ texts. What was the point? They could not understand what he had seen, and he had come to believe that people, any people, were fundamentally untrustworthy. He had trusted Lieutenant Covington, and Covington was dead. He had trusted the platoon’s interpreter, and the interpreter had fled before the shooting started. Now Minh looked at everyone sideways, waiting for the betrayal. At his last family dinner, his cousin asked about Afghanistan and Minh walked out without a word. He could feel himself drifting away from everyone he knew, a separate current pulling him toward somewhere cold and empty. He no longer belonged anywhere—not in the military, not with his family, not in Sacramento. He was a ghost in his own life.

The thing that finally pushed him to call the VA clinic happened three days ago. He was at a stoplight, driving to a shoot, when a motorcycle backfired beside him. In the instant of the bang, Minh saw Lieutenant Covington’s face again, and he was so flooded with rage that he slammed the accelerator and ran the red light, nearly sideswiping a minivan. The driver honked. Minh pulled over, hands trembling, and sat for ten minutes trying to breathe. He realized then that he was dangerous to himself and maybe to others. When he called the intake line, he told the woman he wanted help. What he did not say was that he was terrified the rage would consume him entirely—and that part of him, the part that still heard the lieutenant’s last breath, was not sure he deserved to be saved.
